paper_metadata.title: Carbon market risk estimation using quantum conditional generative adversarial network and amplitude estimation

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid QCGAN‑QAE framework for carbon market risk estimation using EU ETS data (1544 daily prices). A simulated 32‑qubit model encodes loss distributions (8‑qubit output) and estimates VaR/CVaR using QAE with binary search, achieving Δr ≈ 0.94%, 0.83%, and 0.03% at 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence levels respectively, while reporting estimated quantum runtimes of ~0.002 s versus ~168 s for a classical CGAN baseline.

experiments.description: Carbon market risk estimation using a hybrid QCGAN-QAE framework on EU ETS data, including direct QCGAN measurement and QCGAN combined with quantum amplitude estimation plus binary search for VaR/CVaR estimation.

algorithm.variant: Quantum amplitude estimation combined with binary search applied to QCGAN-generated risk distributions
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Training convergence of QCGAN generator/discriminator losses; QAE used for measurement rather than iterative variational convergence
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported for QAE; QCGAN parameters optimized with Adam/COBYLA-based training setup, initial values not specified

optimizer_settings.optimizer: COBYLA for quantum circuits; Adam for GAN training

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Historical loss rates are min-max normalized to [-1,1], divided into 2^8 segments, and converted to binary quantum encoding; 3 days of historical loss rates are encoded as conditional data using 3 x 8 qubits, and the future daily loss rate is encoded with 8 qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate VaR and CVaR of carbon market loss-rate distribution by learning the conditional future loss distribution and measuring tail probabilities
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Binary search over quantum state space to identify VaR threshold; QAE measures cumulative probability mass above threshold

problem_instance.description: EU ETS carbon market risk estimation using daily ECX price data from 2015-01-01 to 2020-12-31
problem_instance.dataset_name: European Union Emissions Trading System / European Climate Exchange (ECX)

dataset_specification.description: Daily carbon prices from European Energy Exchange; third phase of EU carbon market (2013-2020), analysis period 2015-01-01 to 2020-12-31, 1544 data points, no public holidays, 80% train / 20% test split without shuffling

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Compute daily return from price series, negate return to obtain loss rate, min-max normalize loss rates to [-1,1], discretize into 2^8 bins, binary encode, use past 3 days as conditional input
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Backtesting with Kupiec test for VaR and DLC test for CVaR; compare against historical simulation, CGAN, QCGAN, and QCGAN-QAE across 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence levels

implementation_details.classical_solver: Scikit-learn for discriminator; Adam optimizer; COBYLA for quantum circuit optimization
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Pandas and NumPy preprocessing; min-max normalization; binary discretization; train/test split without shuffling
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Decode measured quantum states to loss rates; compute VaR and CVaR; Kupiec and DLC backtests

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: stabilizing losses with reduced oscillation for QCGAN-QAE

speedup_claims.factor: 99.9988% reduction in runtime; about 1/84,500 of CGAN runtime
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper compares quantum-computer time for QCGAN-QAE against traditional-computer time for CGAN; not a like-for-like hardware comparison.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(log N) for VaR search with binary search integrated into QAE; QAE measurement otherwise discussed as reducing from O(N) to O(log N)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(N) for exhaustive QAE-style traversal; classical Monte Carlo requires many simulations

complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: 167-169 s reported for CGAN on traditional computer; 0.0064-0.0122 s for QCGAN-QAE without binary search on quantum computer

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not reported; theoretical complexity O(log N) claimed for VaR search
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require scalable fault‑tolerant QAE circuits and many logical qubits to evaluate large financial distributions; paper only simulates ~32 qubits and does not estimate logical‑qubit resources.
limiting_factors: Experiments performed only in classical simulation (Qiskit)
Speedup comparison uses estimated quantum hardware times rather than measured runtime
Hybrid pipeline requires classical GAN training and classical preprocessing
Input data must be encoded into quantum states (data loading cost not accounted for)
Problem size extremely small (single asset, 1544 data points, discretized into 8‑qubit distribution)
No rigorous classical baseline for amplitude estimation complexity

experiments.description: Comparison of QCGAN circuit architectures: original circuit, modified circuit with swapped entanglement/rotation order, and modified circuit with quantum fully connected (QFC) layer for improved risk distribution generation.

algorithm.optimizer: Adam (GAN training) with parameter‑shift gradient estimation

key_results: Original QCGAN fails Kupiec test at 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence levels (LR values 16.06, 47.47, 109.53).
Modified QCGAN with QFC improves Δr to 3.59%, 0.50%, and 0.29% at 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence levels respectively (Table 4).
CVaR DLC improves from 1.6866 (original) to 0.9882 (modified+QFC) at 90% confidence.

experiments.description: Comparison between direct measurement of QCGAN-generated quantum states and QCGAN combined with Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) for VaR/CVaR estimation.

algorithm.variant: QAE vs direct measurement for risk tail probability estimation

key_results: At 99% confidence level, Δr improves from 0.29% (direct measurement) to 0.03% (QAE).
CVaR DLC improves from 24.9763 to 6.7714 when using QAE (Table 5).
Binary search + QAE reduces quantum runtime from 0.0122 s to 0.0020 s at 90% confidence (Table 6).
